scenes.title: Bealls — composed by AI, every visit
scenes.caption: This is Bealls — a regional retailer with three brands and twelve hundred stores. But there's no theme underneath this storefront. Every section, every product card, every line of copy was generated by an AI engine in real time. The hero, the editorial, the category tiles, the order they appear in — all of it is the output of an inference call, validated against a typed schema, rendered by a foundation that owns the cart and the checkout but nothing visual. This is what happens when the storefront itself is a generated artifact.

scenes.title: Turn on dev mode and the architecture surfaces
scenes.caption: Append a query parameter and the architecture becomes visible. Every zone gets a badge. Red for AI-composed — that's the engine layer. Green for foundation primitives — cart state, navigation, the search box. Blue would be admin-authored content. Gray is a static fallback. Right now the home page is mostly red, with green for the cart icon and the brand strip. Three layers, one repository, every block traceable to the layer that emitted it.

scenes.title: Same catalog. Different shopper signal.
scenes.caption: Switch to the women's category with hunter intent. Same products in the database. Same brand voice. But the layout strategy flips — denser grid, price-rail callout, deal-driven editorial. The engine re-ran persona inference from the URL parameter and recomposed from a different vocabulary subset. The merchant didn't configure a separate hunter landing page. The persona engine and the layout engine are decoupled — one updates beliefs, the other renders from beliefs.

scenes.title: Category pages compose from the same primitives
scenes.caption: Browse to women's clothing. The category page composes from the same vocabulary as home — editorial header, product grid, between-thirds promotion, locator strip — but constrained to PLP latitude. No hero. No category tile grid. Every surface enforces its own composition rules through a typed schema. The AI doesn't break the layout because it can't emit anything the schema doesn't allow.

scenes.title: Refinement by conversation, not filters
scenes.caption: If the AI's read is wrong, the shopper says so. 'Show me casual wear under thirty dollars.' The engine extracts intent tags — casual wear, value-tier — narrows the grid by tag overlap, explains the move in the brand's voice. Each refinement compounds with the previous one. The shopper is co-authoring the storefront through natural language instead of clicking through a filter sidebar.

scenes.title: Product pages — fixed scaffold, AI-composed surroundings
scenes.caption: Open a product. The foundation renders the scaffold — gallery, title, add-to-cart, reviews. Those are not negotiable. Around them, AI-composed zones: pairings sourced from the product's tag-overlap neighborhood, related and recently-viewed pulled from the same retrieval substrate. And up top — the BOPIS strip. Request-aware. Shopper ZIP geocodes to the nearest pickup-ready store. Two-hour ready window. Foundation logic, not AI prose.

scenes.title: Foundation primitives + engine-composed upsell
scenes.caption: Add to cart. The drawer opens. Line items, qty stepper, free-shipping meter, promo code field — all foundation, all read from cart state, instant. The 'Complete your look' row is engine-composed: the AI sources candidates from the cart's tag-overlap neighborhood, picks three pieces that pair with what's in the cart, names the row in brand voice. Foundation owns the contract; the engine writes the merchandising. The split lets the cart never break even if the AI does.

scenes.title: Observe — the operations view
scenes.caption: Switch to the operations side. The Observe dashboard: live signal feed, persona inference per session, every layout generation logged with cost, latency, cache hit rate. This is engine telemetry — the surface an SRE opens during a deploy. It reads from the same Postgres table the merchant Inspector reads from. One signal pipeline, two consumers.

scenes.title: Inside BigCommerce — the merchant control plane
scenes.caption: Now the merchant view. Inside the BigCommerce admin, the Aisles app loads as an embedded iframe. The default tab is the Decisions Inspector. Every layout the AI composed is here — filterable by persona, surface, cache hit. Rows older than this morning predate the data wiring; new rows show brand attribution and persona-distribution percentages. This is the column the merchant cares about most: why.

scenes.title: The why, answered
scenes.caption: Drill into a single decision. Persona inference distribution — gatherer thirty-two percent, hunter twenty-eight, researcher twenty, gifter twenty. Generation latency, model, cost. And below, the explainability narrative: cross-sell zone showed eight products from the seed; top match shared four tags — coastal, casual wear, breathable, daytime — at sixty-seven percent overlap. The merchant gets a complete answer to 'why did the AI do this' without log-diving.

scenes.title: Edit voice without a code deploy
scenes.caption: Brand Voice tab. The merchant edits the AI's voice live. Tone keywords, forbidden terms, the full guidance copy. Publish. Next AI generation reads the override ahead of the brand-config default. No code change, no engineer in the loop. A category manager can update voice between morning standup and the eleven o'clock launch.

scenes.title: Pin the merchandiser's intent
scenes.caption: Persona Fit tab. Pin a product to 'always rank top for hunter persona.' Reason field captures the why — promotional override, end-of-season, exclusive launch. The override surfaces in the Decisions Inspector when applied so the merchandiser's intent is visible end-to-end through the explainability trace. Black-box AI personalization gets transparent and accountable.

scenes.title: Three brands, one admin
scenes.caption: Top right: workspace switcher. One BigCommerce store, three brand workspaces — Bealls, Bealls Florida, Home Centric. Each opens its public storefront in a new tab. Same admin, same Postgres, same engine — three brand personalities. Multi-brand from day one because retrofitting permissions and workspace scoping costs ten times what shipping it on day one does.

scenes.title: Same code, different world
scenes.caption: Click Bealls Florida. Same engine. Same schema. Same enrichment pipeline. But the brand config tells the AI: coastal, family-first, value-driven, Florida vacation aesthetic. The hero adapts. The editorial leans tropical. The product order privileges resort wear. There is no Bealls Florida-specific UI code anywhere in the repository. Adding a brand is a config file, not a feature branch.

scenes.title: Content-mode brand — locator-first
scenes.caption: Third brand: Home Centric. Content mode. No online catalog. The same engine adapts: locator-first hero, in-store events, brand pillars instead of product cards. One mode flag in the brand config and the AI's vocabulary subset shifts accordingly. The schema enforces it — content-mode schemas literally cannot emit transactional blocks. The engine doesn't have to remember; the type system reminds it.

scenes.title: The architecture
scenes.caption: Three layers, one repository. Engine — schema-typed AI composition with a vocabulary of typed blocks and a per-surface latitude rule. Foundation — the always-defined primitives that read state and own the contract with shoppers. Admin — the merchant control plane embedded in BigCommerce, with the Decisions Inspector at the center because explainability is the differentiator. Each layer testable in isolation. Each merchant onboarded by writing one TypeScript brand config. The moat isn't the AI. Anyone can call a language model. The moat is the contract surface that lets one brand ship a storefront without a developer in the loop.
